entities.name: Alexander VI
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Rodrigo de Borja y Borja, who ascended to the papacy as Alexander VI in 1492, was a pivotal and controversial figure of the High Renaissance, serving as head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States until his death in 1503. A member of the influential Borgia family of Aragonese origin, his pontificate was characterized by aggressive political maneuvering, military campaigns to consolidate papal power in central Italy, and notorious nepotism, profoundly shaping the geopolitical landscape of the Italian peninsula and the nascent colonial world.

His tenure saw the infamous Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494, which formally divided the newly discovered lands of the Americas between Spain and Portugal under papal arbitration. Domestically, Alexander VI relentlessly pursued the aggrandizement of his children, most notably Cesare Borgia and Lucrezia Borgia, leveraging the Church's vast resources and his spiritual authority to forge alliances, conduct wars, and secure ducal titles for his progeny. This included military conflicts against powerful Italian families like the Orsini and Colonna, and the controversial suppression of Girolamo Savonarola in Florence.

Alexander VI's papacy left a complex and enduring legacy, accelerating the secularization of the Renaissance papacy and fueling widespread moral critiques that contributed to the climate leading to the Protestant Reformation. His ambitious efforts to establish a dynastic state within the Papal States, though ultimately unsuccessful, illustrated the profound entanglement of spiritual and temporal power in early modern Europe. The Borgia name became synonymous with intrigue, corruption, and ruthless ambition, a perception amplified by contemporary critics and later literary and historical accounts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alexander VI significantly shaped the course of early modern European history by arbitrating the division of the New World through the Treaty of Tordesillas and by intensifying the secularization and political entanglement of the Papacy, which contributed to the pressures leading to the Protestant Reformation.
